language.script_notes: Mexican Spanish. Stop signs read ALTO (not PARE as in South America — a quick continent tell, though Guatemala, Panama and Costa Rica also use ALTO). Speed bumps ('topes') and their warning signs are everywhere. Company names often end in -MEX or -MX (PEMEX, CEMEX, CINEMEX). .mx domain.

road_furniture.bollard_color: White-and-orange bollards are common along highways.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Steel W-beam; concrete barrier on the toll ('cuota') motorways.
road_furniture.line_paint: White edge lines and yellow centre lines; 'topes' (speed bumps) marked with yellow-and-black chevrons or just painted stripes at every town entrance.
road_furniture.curb_style: Painted kerbs, often yellow, in towns.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Concrete utility poles, frequently octagonal in cross-section or shaped like a crucifix. OXXO convenience stores (red/yellow) at almost every junction; blue VeTV satellite dishes on houses; green-and-white highway signage with kilometre markers.

architecture.roof_style: Flat concrete roofs on most houses, cluttered with black plastic water tanks (tinacos) and left-up rebar; clay-tile pitched roofs in the central highlands.
architecture.roof_material: Poured concrete slab; clay tile in the centre; corrugated sheet and palm thatch in the poorer south.
architecture.wall_construction: Unrendered brick or concrete-block, often unfinished with rebar sticking up for a future storey; rendered and brightly painted masonry in finished areas; adobe in the arid north.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Bare grey block and red brick, plus vivid pinks, blues, greens and ochres on painted houses.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Half-finished block houses with rooftop rebar and tinacos; Spanish colonial centres with tiled church domes and cobbled streets; INFONAVIT tract-housing estates on city edges.

nature.vegetation: Desert scrub and cactus in the north; pine-oak forest and agave on the central plateau; tropical dry forest and jungle in the south and on the Yucatán; mangroves on both coasts.
nature.terrain: Two long mountain chains (Sierra Madre Occidental and Oriental) enclosing a high central plateau (the Altiplano), with a volcanic belt across the middle (Popocatépetl, Pico de Orizaba), narrow coastal plains, and a completely flat limestone Yucatán.
nature.climate_signature: Arid and hot in the north, temperate on the high plateau, hot and humid in the tropical south. Wide regional swing — see the regional profiles.

vehicles.plate_color: Each of the 32 states issues its own plate design with the state name across the top — plate colour and graphics are a strong per-state clue (e.g. Jalisco yellow-over-light-blue, Nayarit red). Taxi colours also vary by city — pink in Mexico City, yellow in Monterrey.
vehicles.plate_format: State-dependent, commonly three letters and three–four digits.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Nissan (long the default taxi as the 'Tsuru'), VW (Beetle 'vocho' and Jetta), and pickups everywhere. VW Beetles still common in some regions.

google_coverage.coverage_notes: The Mexican camera car shows no roof bars and no visible wing mirrors — a clean silhouette. Broad coverage nationwide.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Spanish, ALTO stop signs, volcanic highlands, colourful chicken buses, similar architecture along the shared border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Mexican state plates, OXXO stores, 'topes' signage and the bar-and-mirror-free camera car; Guatemala's roads are rougher, its plates uniform, and US-style school buses ('camionetas') dominate.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Desert scenery, wide roads and ranch land continue across the border in the north
confusion_set.tiebreaker: English vs Spanish signage; US state plates and road signs; no OXXO, no topes, no rooftop tinacos or unfinished-rebar houses.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Spanish, mountainous, colonial towns, tropical vegetation
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Colombia's stop signs say PARE, its plates and buses differ, and it has no OXXO or state-name plates.
